cat("> This article needs the packages `multiweb` (`remotes::install_github('lsaravia/multiweb')`) and `igraph`;",
    "they were not available when it was built, so the code is shown without results.\n")

`metaWebNetAssemblyCT()` simulates the assembly of a local food web from a meta-web: species arrive with
rate *m*, go extinct with rate *e*, and predators without prey go extinct with rate *se* (secondary extinction).
Only trophic links matter. `metaWebNetAssemblyML()` extends it to multilayer networks: the non-trophic layers
change the extinction rates, so that

* losing a partner with a **positive** effect (a mutualist, a habitat provider) raises the extinction rate, and
* losing a partner with a **negative** effect (a competitor) lowers it.

The extinction rate of species *i* is

$$e_i(t) = e_i \exp\left(\beta_- f^-_i(t) - \beta_+ f^+_i(t)\right)$$

where $f^+_i(t)$ and $f^-_i(t)$ are the fractions of its positive and negative partners present at time *t*.
$e^{\beta_+}$ and $e^{\beta_-}$ are then the largest factors by which the partners can lower or raise the
extinction rate. Optionally, some species can depend **obligately** on others (e.g. on foundation species): they
go extinct with rate *se* when none of the species they depend on is present, as a predator without prey does.
With $\beta_+ = \beta_- = 0$ and no obligate dependence the model is `metaWebNetAssemblyCT()`.

## The data: a multiplex network of the Chilean rocky intertidal

The `multiweb` package includes the network of Kéfi et al. (2015), with 106 species of the central Chilean rocky
shore and three layers: trophic links, positive non-trophic links (mostly habitat or refuge provision by sessile
species) and negative non-trophic links (mostly competition for space). `multiweb::readMultiplex()` returns an
`mgraph`, a list of igraph layers; the names we give to the layers are their identifiers.

```{r read}
library(meweasmo)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(igraph))

fpath <- system.file("extdata", package = "multiweb")
dn <- list.files(fpath, pattern = "^Kefi2015.*\\.txt$")
dn                                         # files in alphabetical order: negative, positive, trophic
mg <- multiweb::readMultiplex(dn, types = c("Negative", "Positive", "Trophic"), fpath, skipColumn = 2)
sapply(mg, ecount)
```

## The direction of the links

Before simulating we must know what a link `a -> b` means in each layer, because datasets use different
conventions. In these matrices the row species receives the effect of the column species, and `readMultiplex()`
makes links from row to column. In the trophic layer the links therefore go from prey to predator, as
`meweasmo` expects. Basal species have no incoming links:

```{r direction-trophic}
tr <- mg$Trophic
head(V(tr)$name[degree(tr, mode = "in") == 0])
```

In the positive layer the links go from the beneficiary to the species that provides the benefit: the habitat
formers, the mussel *Perumytilus purpuratus* and the kelp *Lessonia nigrescens*, receive the most links.

```{r direction-positive}
head(sort(degree(mg$Positive, mode = "in"), decreasing = TRUE))
```

So the species at the origin of a positive link receives a positive effect and the species at the end none,
(+, 0); in the negative layer the origin receives a negative effect, (-, 0). Competition, recorded in both
directions, becomes (-, -). We write this in a layer table (see `default_layer_signs()` for the format; its
defaults follow a different convention):

```{r layers}
layers <- data.frame(layer     = c("Trophic", "Positive", "Negative"),
                     sign_from = c(-1, 1, -1),
                     sign_to   = c( 1, 0,  0),
                     rule      = c("trophic", "modifier", "modifier"))
```

If the links of a network carry the sign of the effect of `from` on `to` as an edge attribute, use `effect_attr`
instead and the layer signs are not needed.

## From layers to model matrices

`build_multilayer_assembly()` shows how the network is translated: the trophic meta-web `metaW`, the matrix `M` of
effects on the log extinction rate, and the obligate dependence matrix `Dep`.

```{r build}
b <- build_multilayer_assembly(mg, layers, beta = c(pos = 1, neg = 1))
length(b$species)
sum(b$metaW)                                             # trophic links
c(positive_effects = sum(b$M < 0), negative_effects = sum(b$M > 0))
```

`M[i, j]` is the effect of the presence of *j* on the log extinction rate of *i*. With the default
`normalize = TRUE`, each row adds up to at most $-\beta_+$ for the positive partners and $\beta_-$ for the negative
ones. For example, the effects received by the limpet *Scurria variabilis* are:

```{r build-row}
x <- b$M["scurria variabilis", ]
round(x[x != 0], 3)
```

## Simulations

We compare the trophic model ($\beta = 0$) with increasing effects of the non-trophic partners. All species have
the same rates; `metaWebNetAssemblyML()` builds the matrices and simulates.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(123)
tf <- 300
run <- function(beta, ...) metaWebNetAssemblyML(mg, layers, beta = c(pos = beta, neg = beta),
                                                 m = 0.1, e = 0.05, se = 0.5, time = tf, ...)
sims <- lapply(c(0, 1, 2), function(beta) replicate(20, colSums(run(beta)$STime[, 2:(tf - 1)])))
matplot(2:(tf - 1), sapply(sims, rowMeans), type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = c("grey40", "steelblue", "firebrick"),
        xlab = "Time", ylab = "Species present (mean of 20 runs)")
legend("bottomright", c("beta = 0 (trophic only)", "beta = 1", "beta = 2"), lty = 1, lwd = 2,
       col = c("grey40", "steelblue", "firebrick"), bty = "n")
```

Whether the non-trophic layers increase or decrease the number of species depends on the balance between
positive and negative partners. In this network negative links (competition for space) are far more numerous than
positive ones, so stronger effects of the partners lower the number of species. With `normalize = TRUE` the total
effect on each species depends on the *fraction* of its partners present, not on their number.

## Obligate dependence on foundation species

The positive layer is dominated by habitat provision. Suppose the species that receive a positive effect from the
two habitat formers cannot persist without at least one of them:

```{r obligate}
foundation <- c("perumytilus purpuratus", "lessonia nigrescens")
b <- build_multilayer_assembly(mg, layers, beta = c(pos = 1, neg = 1),
                               obligate_on = foundation, obligate_layers = "Positive")
sum(rowSums(b$Dep) > 0)                                  # number of dependent species
```

Half of the species depend on the habitat formers under this rule, a strong assumption; `obligate_layers` and
`obligate_on` control how wide the dependence is.

To see their effect we remove the foundation species from the regional pool (migration rate 0) and compare with
the full pool:

```{r obligate-sim}
m <- ifelse(b$species %in% foundation, 0, 0.1)
S_with <- replicate(20, {
  r <- metaWebNetAssemblyML(mg, layers, beta = c(pos = 1, neg = 1), m = 0.1, e = 0.05, se = 0.5, time = tf,
                            obligate_on = foundation, obligate_layers = "Positive")
  mean(colSums(r$STime[, (tf - 50):(tf - 1)]))
})
S_without <- replicate(20, {
  r <- metaWebNetAssemblyML(mg, layers, beta = c(pos = 1, neg = 1), m = m, e = 0.05, se = 0.5, time = tf,
                            obligate_on = foundation, obligate_layers = "Positive")
  mean(colSums(r$STime[, (tf - 50):(tf - 1)]))
})
boxplot(list("With foundation species" = S_with, "Without foundation species" = S_without),
        ylab = "Species present (last 50 time units)")
```

## Practical notes

* **Check the direction of the links** of every layer before simulating; it is the most common source of silent
  errors. `build_multilayer_assembly()` lets you inspect the result.
* **Parameters.** `beta` is hard to estimate from the structure of a single network. A sensible approach is to fit
  *m*, *e* and *se* (e.g. by ABC on the number of species and the connectance) for each value of `beta` in a grid
  and treat `beta` as a sensitivity parameter.
* **Normalization.** With `normalize = FALSE` the effects add up per partner, and a species with many positive
  partners can become practically immortal.
* **Speed.** For many simulations of the same network, build the matrices once with
  `build_multilayer_assembly()` and call the C++ core `metaWebNetAssemblyMLCT()` directly.

## References

Kéfi, S., Berlow, E. L., Wieters, E. A., Joppa, L. N., Wood, S. A., Brose, U., & Navarrete, S. A. (2015).
Network structure beyond food webs: mapping non-trophic and trophic interactions on Chilean rocky shores.
*Ecology*, 96(1), 291–303. https://doi.org/10.1890/13-1424.1
